title: DTE Energy To Sell DTE Vantage Business For $3 Billion To J.P. Morgan Asset Management Investors And Expand Utility Investments To $44 Billion - Pulse 2.0
content: DTE Energy, a Detroit-based electric and natural gas utility company, has entered into an agreement to sell all of its non-utility DTE Vantage business substantially for approximately $3 billion to institutional investors advised by the Global Infrastructure group at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The transaction will support DTE’s strategy of concentrating on regulated utility operations and expanding infrastructure investments across Michigan. The sale is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions. The transaction includes substantially all DTE Vantage assets, excluding EES Coke. DTE plans to direct additional resources toward its electric and natural gas utilities, which serve approximately 2.3 million electric customers in Southeast Michigan and 1.4 million natural gas customers statewide. The company outlined approximately $44 billion in customer-focused capital investments planned over the next five years, including projects involving grid modernization, reliability improvements, cleaner electricity generation, and infrastructure supporting growing energy demand. Through the first nine months of 2026, DTE invested nearly $4.1 billion in its regulated utilities and remains on track to invest approximately $6.1 billion during the full year. The planned divestiture also comes as DTE expands its infrastructure to accommodate demand from hyperscale data centers. Following approval from the Michigan Public Service Commission, DTE is moving forward with energy supply agreements supporting two hyperscale data center customers in Michigan, including Google’s planned facility in Van Buren Township. DTE expects the agreements to generate substantial financial benefits for existing utility customers through 2045. Under the contracts, data center operators will cover the full cost of the electricity supply and grid investments required to serve their facilities. The company also expects the data centers to contribute billions of dollars to the electric system, helping reduce the share of system costs paid by existing customers. The agreements are intended to support economic development while protecting current ratepayers from infrastructure expenses associated with large new electricity consumers. DTE has also filed a 20-year Integrated Resource Plan with the Michigan Public Service Commission outlining its proposed approach to future electricity generation. The plan combines renewable energy, battery storage, nuclear power, and natural gas generation to meet changing electricity demand while maintaining reliability and managing customer costs. DTE remains committed to ending coal-fired electricity generation by 2032. Its latest resource plan targets an 84% reduction in carbon dioxide emissions and is projected to cost approximately $3.5 billion less than the company’s previous plan. The utility also completed the 100-megawatt Cold Creek Solar Park near Coldwater, Michigan, through its renewable energy partnership with Ford Motor Company. The project supports Ford’s objective of assembling every vehicle manufactured in Michigan using the equivalent of 100% carbon-free electricity by the end of 2027. At the end of 2025, DTE operated 20 wind parks and 34 solar parks, collectively generating enough electricity to power more than 900,000 homes. The company also reported providing customers with access to nearly $125 million in energy assistance during 2025. Alongside the DTE Vantage sale announcement, DTE reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $470 million, or $2.25 per diluted share, compared with $419 million, or $2.01 per share, during the prior-year quarter. Operating earnings increased to $481 million, or $2.30 per share, from $468 million, or $2.25 per share, in the third quarter of 2025. For the first nine months of 2026, DTE reported net income of $999 million, compared with $1.09 billion during the corresponding period in 2025. The company confirmed its full-year 2026 operating earnings guidance of $7.59 to $7.73 per share and provided a 2027 pro forma operating earnings baseline within the same range, reflecting the proposed DTE Vantage divestiture. Lazard is serving as exclusive financial advisor to DTE Energy on the sale, while Kirkland & Ellis is providing legal counsel. The transaction represents a significant portfolio restructuring for DTE, allowing the company to narrow its focus on regulated utility services while advancing an expanded investment program designed to support Michigan’s long-term electricity and natural gas requirements. “DTE Vantage has been a strong non-utility business and valued part of DTE Energy for more than 30 years. This transaction advances our strategy to focus our resources on our regulated electric and gas utilities, where we see significant opportunities to invest on behalf of customers and communities. The sale supports our plan to deliver meaningful affordability benefits for customers, strengthens our ability to execute a substantial utility investment plan and positions DTE as a high-growth, premium utility with a stronger long-term outlook.” “Strong financial performance through the third quarter of 2026 positions us to continue investing in Michigan’s energy infrastructure while delivering long-term value for our customers, communities and shareholders.” Thank you for visiting Pulse 2.0. title: Double-digit price declines in property cat reinsurance likely to persist, says JP Morgan - Reinsurance News
content:
JP Morgan, the US-based global investment bank and financial services company, expects double-digit price declines in property catastrophe reinsurance to persist into 2027, as strong industry profitability, relatively low natural catastrophe losses and an influx of capital continue to put pressure on rates. The reinsurance market, and notably property and property cat lines, have been experiencing softer pricing conditions for some time, but 2026 marked an acceleration in the pace of reductions. Following a period of exceptionally high rates in 2023 and 2024 after the so-called reset, pricing has moved progressively lower, with more substantial decreases recorded across the latest renewal periods. JP Morgan cited figures from reinsurance broker Marsh Re, formerly known as Guy Carpenter, showing that average reinsurance prices declined by approximately 12% at the January 2026 renewals. The downward trend continued into the mid-year renewal period, with global property catastrophe rates falling by 16% at the July 2026 renewals. The investment bank anticipates additional pricing pressure at the January 2027 renewals, particularly within property catastrophe lines, where it expects double-digit decreases to continue. JP Morgan attributed this outlook to several factors, including the sector’s sustained strong returns on equity (ROE), relatively benign catastrophe experience during 2026 to date and the availability of new sources of capital. JP Morgan noted that reinsurers have recorded particularly favourable financial results since 2023, with average ROEs remaining in the high teens. The bank compared this performance with the period following Hurricane Katrina, when increased property catastrophe rates and elevated interest rates supported similarly strong industry returns. However, the investment bank cautioned that extended periods of consistently high profitability have been relatively uncommon in the reinsurance industry. Historically, fluctuations in catastrophe losses have contributed to greater volatility in earnings than has been observed in recent years, suggesting that the current level of profitability may become harder to sustain. JP Morgan also indicated that the financial consequences of declining reinsurance rates are beginning to emerge, particularly in underwriting performance, despite the sector’s continued resilience in the near term. The bank pointed to Munich Re as one of the first major reinsurers to demonstrate the effects of weaker pricing on its combined ratio expectations during 2026. At the beginning of the year, Munich Re’s normalised combined ratio was expected to stand at 80%, but this had deteriorated to approximately 82% by the second quarter. While other reinsurers have so far experienced a more limited impact, JP Morgan believes the broader industry will find it increasingly difficult to offset continued rate reductions. The bank therefore expects underwriting margins to face growing pressure over the next two years as lower pricing gradually affects financial performance. title: JPM Flags Higher Rate Risks: Can Its Balance Sheet Stay Resilient? - The Globe and Mail
content: JPMorgan JPM remains focused on maintaining balance sheet resilience amid expectations of structurally higher interest rates. At the Nov. 5 BancAnalysts Association of Boston Conference, Charles Bristow, head of Treasury and chief investment officer, emphasized disciplined duration management, stable operating deposits and rigorous stress testing to navigate interest rate volatility.Bristow noted that JPMorgan has historically avoided excessive exposure to longer-duration securities, helping limit valuation risks as interest rates increased. Its emphasis on operating deposits linked to payments, custody and checking activities also supports funding stability, although unusually sharp rate increases could pressure deposit costs.The company's underlying performance reinforces this resilience. During the first nine months of 2026, reported net interest income (NII) increased 11% year over year to $77.9 billion. NII excluding Markets rose 4% to $71.7 billion, supported by deposit and loan growth. JPMorgan expects fourth-quarter 2026 NII of approximately $28 billion, implying full-year NII of $106.2 billion, while NII excluding Markets is projected to be $97.2 billion. Its preliminary 2027 outlook projects NII excluding Markets of nearly $107 billion, reflecting almost 10% growth backed by balance sheet expansion and higher rates.However, Bristow cautioned that proposed regulatory capital requirements could undermine returns from certain low-risk intermediation activities. Rapid interest rate repricing and tighter systemwide liquidity also pose risks. Overall, JPMorgan's diversified franchise, disciplined asset-liability management and stable deposit base support its earnings outlook. Nevertheless, regulatory uncertainty, funding costs and interest rate volatility warrant monitoring, suggesting a balanced investment approach. Two close peers of JPMorgan are Bank of AmericaBAC and Citigroup C.Bank of America is well-positioned to benefit from higher interest rates, supported by its asset-sensitive balance sheet, fixed-rate asset repricing and loan growth. Bank of America expects 2026 NII to increase approximately 8% year over year. However, higher deposit costs could partly offset these benefits.Citigroup is positioned to benefit from higher interest rates, given its asset-sensitive balance sheet, loan growth and investment portfolio repricing. Citigroup expects 2026 NII, excluding Markets, to increase in the mid-to-high 6% range year over year. However, rising deposit costs could partly offset these benefits. Every fall, the world's biggest money managers publish return forecasts that pension funds, endowments and financial advisers use to decide what goes in a portfolio. Being included in one of those tables is a quiet sign that an asset is being taken seriously. Bitcoin made it into one this year. Now Grayscale is laying out why the numbers behind that matter. In a Nov. 4 note, Zach Pandl, Head of Research at Grayscale, called Bitcoin's inclusion in JPMorgan Asset Management's 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions "another milestone in its evolution as an institutional asset." Related: Democratic sweep leaves crypto bill weeks to live The report is JPMorgan's 31st annual edition, and it projects returns over the next 10 to 15 years. TheStreet Roundtable reported last month that the report gives Bitcoin a base-case return of about 10% a year, the highest of any asset in the forecast. Pandl's note looks past that figure. Pandl focuses on correlation, which measures how closely two assets move together. JPMorgan estimates Bitcoin's correlation with U.S. large-cap stocks at 33%. That is lower than international equities, corporate bonds and hedge funds, according to a Grayscale chart based on the report. title: The blue wave is changing the AI trade - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. The U.S. economy and the stock market have proven resilient in 2026, even in the face of higher interest rates, geopolitical volatility and yet another energy shock. Whereas the U.S. consumer, aided by fiscal stimulus and tax cuts, is still spending, a growing driver of GDP growth remains the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. In the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, the Democratic party gained control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, setting the stage for gridlock with a Republican president—especially when it comes to the continued development and adoption of AI across the country. Investors feared a federal moratorium that mirrors some of the state-led initiatives to curb the build-out, in response to affordability and zoning concerns. So, it’s only natural that the outcome of the elections initially sent stock market futures plunging nearly 2% before rebounding with significant volatility in technology companies even days after the result. Democratic gains increase the likelihood of tougher scrutiny around data center development, electricity affordability and who pays for new grid infrastructure. This can create near-term uncertainty for sectors that trade in line with AI developments like utilities—especially those with exposure to fast-growing markets like Texas and Georgia that offer affordable land, labor and both energy and water access. Even as investors reprice that risk, the structural backdrop remains in place. Hyperscaler investment is expected to continue. Electrification and the grid build-out are still pressing needs in order to support higher power demand and capital spending. Stopping the data center build-out is still a tall order. Initial efforts to curb the data center build-out began over the summer. Any new policies to slow or restrict new connections would build on a process that’s already underway. More notable policy changes could be around who bears the costs of additional grid connections, changes to tax exemptions, stricter financial commitments and emergency curtailment requirements, among others. While much of this uncertainty was priced in leading into the elections, the magnitude of the Democratic gains was not. And that’s changing the nature of the tech trade underneath the hood. In an environment where regulation could change even if the most AI-friendly states, companies with existing compute and data center projects—like the hyperscalers—have the edge. Plus, additional regulatory proposals target new developments, not existing ones, which could strengthen the position of companies with operational data centers, secured power and established customers. Combined with any potential moderation in AI growth and the ability to meet greater construction and permitting standards, the established lead that some of the biggest tech companies have is even more beneficial relative to the parts of the tech trade that rely on the incremental build-out. And that’s something investors are already pricing, sending the message that owning productive capacity today is different from depending on its construction tomorrow—even if that means factoring in potential regulatory risk. Before the policy details have even been settled, or formally proposed, investors have already repriced these possibilities. It’s most visible in parts of the “picks and shovels” AI infrastructure trade—the part of the market that rallied on the certainty of the build-out even as the return on investment faced remain in question. The 24-month forward price-to-earnings ratio of the MVIS US Listed Semiconductor Index has halved since June. After trading at a peak of 22.5 times forward earnings in June, the index currently trades at 11.4 times forward earnings. That’s at a valuation lower than when investors were digesting the beginning of the conflict in Iran, Liberation Day and the stock market lows of 2022. It reflects a market questioning the durability of the industry’s earnings and continued growth in capital expenditures. But that’s where the opportunity may lie. Yes, regulation is subject to change, but the scale of economic growth that has come from this sector alone may bear some impact on the level and willingness to limit continued development. The AI trade is far from over, but it is evolving. Financing, regulatory and power constraints can mean a bumpy road ahead, but unless end demand falters, the risk of an inventory overhang and earnings slowdown may already be baked into valuations. As the structural backdrop of the AI build-out remains in place, the key is to determine which companies have the lead in an undeniable technological evolution that can broaden out in the years to come. The U.S. economy and the stock market have proven resilient in 2026, even in the face of higher interest rates, geopolitical volatility and yet another energy shock. Whereas the U.S. consumer, aided by fiscal stimulus and tax cuts, is still spending, a growing driver of GDP growth remains the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. In the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, the Democratic party gained control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, setting the stage for gridlock with a Republican president—especially when it comes to the continued development and adoption of AI across the country. Investors feared a federal moratorium that mirrors some of the state-led initiatives to curb the build-out, in response to affordability and zoning concerns. So, it’s only natural that the outcome of the elections initially sent stock market futures plunging nearly 2% before rebounding with significant volatility in technology companies even days after the result. Democratic gains increase the likelihood of tougher scrutiny around data center development, electricity affordability and who pays for new grid infrastructure. This can create near-term uncertainty for sectors that trade in line with AI developments like utilities—especially those with exposure to fast-growing markets like Texas and Georgia that offer affordable land, labor and both energy and water access. Even as investors reprice that risk, the structural backdrop remains in place. Hyperscaler investment is expected to continue. Electrification and the grid build-out are still pressing needs in order to support higher power demand and capital spending. Stopping the data center build-out is still a tall order. Initial efforts to curb the data center build-out began over the summer. Any new policies to slow or restrict new connections would build on a process that’s already underway. More notable policy changes could be around who bears the costs of additional grid connections, changes to tax exemptions, stricter financial commitments and emergency curtailment requirements, among others. While much of this uncertainty was priced in leading into the elections, the magnitude of the Democratic gains was not. And that’s changing the nature of the tech trade underneath the hood. In an environment where regulation could change even if the most AI-friendly states, companies with existing compute and data center projects—like the hyperscalers—have the edge. Plus, additional regulatory proposals target new developments, not existing ones, which could strengthen the position of companies with operational data centers, secured power and established customers. Combined with any potential moderation in AI growth and the ability to meet greater construction and permitting standards, the established lead that some of the biggest tech companies have is even more beneficial relative to the parts of the tech trade that rely on the incremental build-out. And that’s something investors are already pricing, sending the message that owning productive capacity today is different from depending on its construction tomorrow—even if that means factoring in potential regulatory risk. Before the policy details have even been settled, or formally proposed, investors have already repriced these possibilities. It’s most visible in parts of the “picks and shovels” AI infrastructure trade—the part of the market that rallied on the certainty of the build-out even as the return on investment faced remain in question. The 24-month forward price-to-earnings ratio of the MVIS US Listed Semiconductor Index has halved since June. After trading at a peak of 22.5 times forward earnings in June, the index currently trades at 11.4 times forward earnings. That’s at a valuation lower than when investors were digesting the beginning of the conflict in Iran, Liberation Day and the stock market lows of 2022. It reflects a market questioning the durability of the industry’s earnings and continued growth in capital expenditures. But that’s where the opportunity may lie. Yes, regulation is subject to change, but the scale of economic growth that has come from this sector alone may bear some impact on the level and willingness to limit continued development. The AI trade is far from over, but it is evolving. Financing, regulatory and power constraints can mean a bumpy road ahead, but unless end demand falters, the risk of an inventory overhang and earnings slowdown may already be baked into valuations. As the structural backdrop of the AI build-out remains in place, the key is to determine which companies have the lead in an undeniable technological evolution that can broaden out in the years to come. title: Democrats to probe JPMorgan's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein when they take Senate control - CNBC
content:
Senate Democrats are gearing up to investigate JPMorgan Chase’s banking relationship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein once they take control of Congress early next year. Democratic staffers on the Senate Finance Committee intend to home in on how high-ranking executives at JPMorgan handled Epstein, a source familiar with the panel’s thinking told CNBC on Thursday. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because the probe of the nation’s biggest bank has not been announced. The Finance Committee is likely to be chaired beginning in January by Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat who currently is the panel’s ranking member. Wyden has made clear he plans to make full use of the subpoena powers that committee majorities wield. Democratic staffers aim to focus in particular on decisions about Epstein made by Mary Callahan Erdoes, the CEO of JPMorgan’s asset and wealth management division, the source said. JPMorgan declined to comment. The bank has previously said it regrets any association with Epstein but that it did not assist him in committing crimes. In a 2023 deposition, Erdoes said she was aware as early as 2006 that Epstein was accused of paying cash to have underage girls brought to his home. Epstein had been a client of the bank since 1998. Epstein became a registered sex offender after pleading guilty in 2008 in Florida to a state criminal charge of procuring an underage girl for prostitution. JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon in his own, later deposition in 2023, said Erdoes had authority to cut off Epstein as a client. She did not take that step until 2013. Epstein, a former friend of President Donald Trump, ex-President Bill Clinton and many other high-profile people, died in a jailhouse suicide in August 2019, weeks after being arrested on federal child sex trafficking charges. A lawyer for the U.S. Virgin Islands told a federal judge in New York in 2023 that JPMorgan “was a full-service bank for Jeffrey Epstein’s sex trafficking,” and that it waited until after he killed himself to notify the Treasury Department of $1 billion in suspicious transactions related to trafficking by Epstein. “This was a CYA [cover your a--] reporting after 16 years of all of the monies flowing in his JPMorgan accounts after he was dead,” the lawyer, Mimi Liu, said. JPMorgan has blamed former investment banking chief Jes Staley for concealing or failing to report criminal activity related to Epstein, with whom he had a close relationship. Staley, who left JPMorgan in 2013 and later became CEO of Barclays before stepping down in 2021, has denied knowledge of Epstein’s crimes. House Oversight Chair James Comer, R-Ky., after a closed-door interview with Staley in July, said that the former executive had encouraged JPMorgan to keep Epstein as a client. In mid-2023, JPMorgan agreed to a $290 million settlement with victims of Epstein without admitting wrongdoing. That same year, JPMorgan agreed to pay $75 million to settle a separate lawsuit by the U.S. Virgin Islands alleging that the bank facilitated and benefited from the sex trafficking of young women by Epstein. In August, Wyden released a report accusing top officials at multiple banks of “looking the other way” as Epstein moved hundreds of millions of dollars to finance a yearslong sex trafficking operation. “The report exposes how top bankers shielded Epstein from federal scrutiny by delaying the reporting of Epstein’s suspicious financial activity to the U.S. government, likely in violation of federal anti-money-laundering laws,” Wyden’s office said in a statement that month. “It includes new details about the extent of suspicious activity reported by Deutsche Bank after Epstein’s death, new details from bank reports filed about suspicious transfers to Epstein through accounts at Bank of America, and names top officials at JPMorgan Chase and other banks who were responsible for reporting Epstein’s shady activities to the government but instead protected Epstein in order to gain access to Leon Black and other billionaires.” Black, former CEO of Apollo Global Management, was revealed to have paid Epstein $158 million for financial advice in the years after his 2008 conviction. In September, Black sued the House oversight panel, seeking to block subpoenas it had issued him for his testimony and for documents related to its Epstein probe. On Wednesday, Black sued Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to become chair of the Oversight Committee in the next Congress, alleging Garcia defamed him in statements regarding Epstein. The lawsuit focuses on Garcia’s claims in a TV interview that Black “is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes” and “was one of the last people to actually interact” with Epstein before his death, among others. The Department of Justice’s mountain of files related to Epstein became a major focus in late 2025 and early 2026, after Congress passed a bill ordering the DOJ to make those records public. Trump’s name is referenced thousands of times in the files that have been released. The president has not been charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein, with whom he fell out in the early 2000s. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. title: J.P. Morgan Snags Merrill Lifer Managing $940 Million in Los Angeles - AdvisorHub
content: J.P. Morgan Wealth Management on Friday hired a Merrill Lynch lifer who managed $940 million in assets in Los Angeles, according to an announcement from the hiring firm. J. Tiffany Yu, who first registered with the thundering herd in 1998, joined an existing team at J.P. Morgan Advisors in Century City, according to the announcement. The team, Elevate Wealth Partners, is led by advisor Eric Gray and includes two other advisors and five support staff. Yu and members of the team did not respond to a request for comment. “Her hire builds on our established presence in the Los Angeles community and strengthens our ability to meet growing client demand there,” Michael Rogers, Los Angeles regional director, said in a statement. J.P. Morgan earlier this year added other advisors in California, including David Amar, who managed $1.1 billion in Los Angeles at William Blair, and Pourya Naeimi, who oversaw $533 million in Palo Alto at Wells Fargo, according to the announcement. They report to Mollie Colavita, a former Merrill Private Wealth manager who took over as head of J.P. Morgan’s wealth unit in September 2025. Naeimi, who joined in September, was one of Colavita’s first hires in the region since taking over. Colavita’s predecessor, Phil Sieg, had set a target in 2021 to more than double the headcount at J.P. Morgan Advisors to around 1,000 from 450. Thanks to its parent bank’s purchase of First Republic’s private wealth unit in 2023, headcount jumped to around 600, although the firm has also suffered some large departures. Last month, two of its top teams, who managed $18.6 billion in assets combined, launched an RIA. Meanwhile, J.P. Morgan also last month hired former Merrill Lynch Private Wealth regional leader Linda A. Patel to be head of its Southeast territory based in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. She also reports to Colavita and succeeds Janet Sweeney, a 40-year industry veteran who retired earlier this year. A Merrill spokesperson also did not respond to a request for comment. The group is anchored by a Merrill team with around $1.8 billion in assets.

JPMorgan JPM is strengthening its payments franchise through automation and blockchain technology. On Nov. 2, its J.P. Morgan Payments division launched Receivables Matching, a solution that automates reconciliation across incoming payments, remittance information and outstanding receivables.The solution reduces manual processing, accelerates cash application and enhances cash-flow visibility. Its effectiveness is reflected in Grimco's experience, with the distributor reporting more than 60% lower manual review time and approximately 95% fewer errors requiring manual intervention.The launch complements JPMorgan's broader digital payments initiatives, particularly its blockchain platform, Kinexys. The platform facilitates round-the-clock, near-real-time cross-border settlements and programmable payments, helping corporate clients streamline treasury operations and optimize liquidity management.Kinexys has gained significant traction, processing more than $4 trillion in cumulative transactions and averaging $7 billion daily as of September 2026. Its expanding capabilities, including multicurrency blockchain deposit accounts, underscore growing institutional interest in blockchain-enabled financial infrastructure.These initiatives highlight JPMorgan's focus on reducing payment-processing complexities and enhancing transaction efficiency. By strengthening its digital treasury capabilities, JPMorgan could attract corporate clients, deepen existing relationships and unlock cross-selling opportunities.These developments may reinforce its competitive position and support long-term Payments revenue growth, which touched $16 billion in the first nine months of 2026. However, the financial benefits will depend on broader adoption and successful commercialization amid intensifying competition in digital payments. Two close peers of JPMorgan are Bank of America BAC and Citigroup C.Bank of America is expanding its Payments business through cross-border real-time payments, CashPro enhancements, APIs and AI-driven treasury solutions. content: Treasury/cash management FinTech Embat has launched a new partnership with J.P. Morgan Payments. Embat announced Wednesday (Nov. 4) that it has integrated J.P. Morgan’s new banking authorization service (BAS) API for treasury services and payments, letting joint clients connect their J.P. Morgan bank accounts to Embat’s treasury management platform. “Traditionally, connecting a treasury platform to a bank requires obtaining certificates through an external certification authority,” Embat said in a news release provided to PYMNTS. “This often requires extensive implementation time, data validation and signatures—a process that can take months before a client can begin operations.” The new integration lets joint clients authenticate and connect their J.P. Morgan bank accounts to Embat’s treasury platform in seconds, with no IT development needed. This streamlines client account activation and means less operational effort for treasury teams. “The integration is particularly beneficial for organisations with multiple subsidiaries or entities, as they no longer need to replicate the bank connection process for each legal entity,” the release added. “Leveraging J.P. Morgan Payments’ single multi-tenant certificate management connection—a single security setup that safely covers multiple subsidiaries – enables finance teams to onboard and manage all corporate entities easily. “ Embat said it will be the first treasury management system to leverage J.P. Morgan Payments’ own user interface through the company’s API integration. Antonio Berga, Embat’s co-founder and co-CEO, added that the partnership eliminates the “time-consuming and tedious” bank connectivity processes. “What used to take months is now operational within days, with no technical development required,” Berga said. “Clients simply sign the legal documentation authorizing Embat to access their accounts. Once they go live, they have the benefit of making decisions based on real-time data, backed by Embat’s AI technology and the robustness and security of a top-tier bank.” Writing about treasury management in late September, PYMNTS argued that the key shift in this space is not from manual to AI treasury, but from observation to execution. “Financial software spent years aggregating information that previously lived across bank portals, spreadsheets and enterprise systems,” the report said. “The next generation is being asked to interpret those signals. After all, once software can understand that a company has $30 million sitting in one account, a large obligation approaching somewhere else and receivables expected later in the day, the obvious question becomes. Why stop at generating an alert?” The report also cites data from PYMNTS Intelligence’s “SMB Growth Monitor: How Firms Use and Choose Credit Cards,” showing that when small- to medium-sized businesses were asked about factors affecting their choice of a primary corporate card, 15.7% pointed to “better card and spending analytics” and 13.8% mentioned “allows for better expense management.” Revolving Debt Jumps as Spending Strains Credit Cards BMO Turns to Agentic AI to Resolve Card Issues Sysco Counts on AI Routing and Bidding for $500 Million in Savings Study Finds Most Stablecoins Fail GENIUS Act Requirements
